b: One of my favourite studies of investment behaviour comes from Fidelity. An internal audit of client investor account activity from 2003 to 2013 found that the most successful cohort of investors were the dead ones.
Dead people are not influenced by the latest research. They are immune to the euphoria of market bubbles, and they do not panic when markets fall.
However, there is one small flaw in the Fidelity research.
It doesn’t exist. Despite being widely referenced, there is no evidence that the analysis was ever done.

The myth appears to have taken root from a Bloomberg Radio interview with the investment manager James O’Shaughnessy. He recounted some supposed Fidelity findings about the superior performance of dormant accounts, prompting the interviewer to joke that perhaps the investors were dead.

The longevity of the myth suggests there is something in this notion that we find appealing, all the same. It feels instinctively true that in most cases the best thing to do with your investments is nothing – that continual fiddling will hurt your returns.
So is there any real research to back this up?
There is certainly strong evidence that higher trading frequency can lead to lower returns.
A US study by Barber and Odean in 2000, Trading is Hazardous to Your Wealth, looked at the trading activity on over 60,000 household investing accounts at a large discount broker.
The average annual return for the fifth quintile who traded the most was 11.4%
Across all accounts the average annual return was 16.4%

You may be thinking that 11.4% still sounds like a decent return. But the study covered the period from 1991 to 1996 – a boom time for US stocks that culminated in Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan’s famous warning about ‘irrational exuberance’. Against the market returns available during this period, that 11.4% was distinctly modest.
The authors argue that overconfidence encourages investors to trade more frequently, often resulting in lower returns. They conclude:
Our central message is that trading is hazardous to your wealth.
I suspect there are very few Monevator readers who are tempted to act like a meme stock day trader, however.
What about something more pedestrian? Perhaps an occasional, carefully considered switch between funds?
The evidence warns against this, too.
The 2026 Mind The Gap US report from Morningstar examined the returns earned by US retail investors choosing to put their money in a range of mutual funds and ETFs in the 10 years to the end of 2025.

The report explored the difference in returns between a hypothetical investment left untouched in a fund for the entire ten years, versus the return of actual investors taking into account when they bought and sold.
While the average annual return of the hypothetical investment was 9.9%, the estimated return for investors was 8.7%.

Morningstar attributes this gap of 1.2 percentage points primarily to the timing of investor trades. Hence its findings suggest that investors may improve their returns by simply leaving their investments alone.
Now, some researchers have previously criticised the report, arguing that alternative methods of analysis produce a much smaller gap.
But hey – at least the research exists this time!
Passive investors need very few funds in their toolkit. This naturally limits the temptation to switch between a multitude of shiny top-quartile funds.
Mostly they just need to decide on their asset allocation percentages. So is it safe to fiddle with those settings?

Jeffrey Ptak at Morningstar attempted to answer this question by examining the returns of tactical allocation funds. These are funds that frequently change asset allocation in an attempt to exploit prevailing market conditions.

Ptak compared the average return of tactical allocation funds over the decade to March 2025 with that of a hypothetical portfolio based on their average asset allocation in 2015, left unchanged over the following decade.
Or, as he puts it, if the fund managers had simply gone fishing instead.
Over the ten years, a $10,000 investment in the average tactical allocation fund would have increased to $14,524.
The same money invested in the ‘do nothing’ fund would have increased to $21,113.

Ptak also compared the performance over rolling three-year periods from the start of each month throughout the decade. The ‘do nothing’ portfolio was based on the average asset allocation as at the start of each of these three-year periods.
You guessed it: in 81 of the 85 three-year periods, the ‘do nothing’ portfolio had a better return than the average tactical allocation fund.

All this evidence suggests that trying to anticipate market conditions can be counterproductive. And that highly paid fund managers using clever analysis to fiddle on your behalf can be just as bad for your returns.
Each study has its drawbacks, of course. You can pick holes in the sample periods, fees, and methodologies.
But across three different kinds of activity the broad conclusion is the same: doing less usually wins.
Of course, some changes to a portfolio are perfectly sensible.

Neither rebalancing to predetermined asset allocation percentages nor an intentional increase in cash holdings in the run-up to retirement to try to manage sequence of returns risk could reasonably be described as fiddling.
On the other hand, if you buy a stock after a tip on social media or sell assets when you read a news story about today’s market falls then you have clearly strayed well into fiddling territory.
But between such signposts, things are not so clear cut.
Say you buy into an investment trust after you notice that its discount has widened to 20%. Are you fiddling?
That depends. Was exploiting discounts already part of your long-term investment plan? Or was it just a whim?
An investment plan, preferably written down, should explain what you’re trying to achieve and how you intend to achieve it.
If you don’t have a plan, then it’s easy to drift into fiddling.
How about a switch in asset allocation to the Permanent Portfolio weightings after reading some compelling analysis from Monevator?
This would be a radical change to your investment plan.

Of course, plans can and sometimes should change. But a good investment plan is designed to see you through years of ups and downs – ideally decades. It won’t help if you change horses every couple of years.

It’s very easy to fool yourself with this kind of decision. You can convince yourself that your change of heart has nothing to do with prevailing market conditions, that you’ve finally seen the light, and that you’ll stick with this new plan forever.
At least until next month when you read about the Golden Butterfly Portfolio or some other shiny new strategy.
An old investing aphorism (often attributed to the economist Eugene Fama) sums all this up rather well:
Your money is like a bar of soap – the more you handle it, the less you’ll have.
So how do you guard against the slippery temptation to fiddle? A few simple rules could help:
Have a plan and write it down
Don’t rush into changes – give yourself time to think
The last of these is the most important and, unfortunately, it’s the hardest.
Of course you will still be tempted to fiddle. You’re only human. But when in doubt, you know what to do.
